about: Fourteen laws on the family. The first punishes a man who accuses a woman of misconduct and cannot prove it (§127): he is thrown down before the judges and half (of his hair) is shaved. A marriage whose contracts have not been set is no marriage (§128). Then the adultery laws: a wife caught with another man is bound and thrown into the water with him, unless her husband spares her and the king spares his servant (§129); a man who holds down a man’s wife who has not known a male and lives in her father’s house is killed, and the woman is released (§130). A wife merely accused by her husband swears the oath of the god and goes home (§131); one only spoken against must plunge into the River for her husband’s sake (§132). Next the captivity laws: a wife whose husband has been carried off may stay in her house, and if there is food she must (§133, partly restored), if she goes elsewhere she is thrown into the water (§133A), but if there is no food she bears no blame (§134); if she has borne children in the other house, she goes back to her first husband when he returns, and the sons follow their own father (§135); a man who abandons his city loses his wife (§136). The last laws are on divorce: a man who divorces a wife who has borne him children gives her back her dowry and half the field, orchard and goods, and she raises the children, takes a share like one heir’s, and marries whom she likes (§137); one who divorces a childless wife gives her her bride-price and dowry (§138); and where there was no bride-price, a mina of silver, or a third of a mina if he is a commoner (§139–140). Harper’s transliteration is followed. Lines XXII 12–17 are broken and printed in brackets: they are Harper’s restorations, not stone. Several words are uncertain and are said so in the notes: ugbabtum, šugītum, the restored pagarša, the verbs urabbâ and urtabbû, uzubbûm and ḫāwirum.

sentences.i: If a man has had a finger pointed at an ugbabtum (a priestess?) or at another man’s wife, and has not proved it,
sentences.n: The slander laws begin, and the first is one long “if”. Read it clause by clause: eli “against, at”, then two women, then the verb. ubānam ušatrīṣma is “he made a finger point”, the code’s idiom for an accusation: ubānum “finger”, ušatrīṣ the Š-stem of tarāṣum “to stretch out, point” (the t is part of the root), with -ma “and”. lā uktīn is “he did not prove (it)”, the D-stem of kânum, the same verb as ukannūšuma in §112. aššat is aššatum “wife” in the construct state, “the wife of” a man. The conjunction u is written ù. The sign group read ugbabtum is UNCERTAIN: Harper prints NIN.AN here and gives it no reading, and the plate agrees with his print. After e-li it shows the hexagon sign with the small boxed-wedge sign that together spell NIN, and then AN; the second hexagon with its long tail, which stands in front of them at XVIII 36 (§110, where the group is ŠAL.NIN.AN), is not there, so no ŠAL is written. It is read ugbabtum, a priestess, as in §110, which is no more certain. The code never reads it nadītum.

sentences.i: they shall throw that man down before the judges and shave half (of his hair).
sentences.n: The apodosis. Both verbs are plural with no subject written: “they” means the court. inaddûšu is nadûm “to throw, cast down” with -šu “him” (nadûm, not nadānum “to give”: the weak ending -û shows it). maḫar dajjānī is “before the judges”. muttassu is Harper’s mu-ut-ta-zu: muttatum is “half” (it returns in §137 as muttat eqlim, “half of the field”) and -zu is -šu after the t, said -ssu, so “his half”; the hair is understood, not written. ugallabū is the D-stem of galābum “to shave”, plural, “they shall shave”. The penalty is shame in public, not death.

sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and has not set down her contracts, that woman is not a wife.
sentences.n: A short law with a two-part “if” and a flat verdict with no verb at all: zinništum šī ul aššat is “that woman — not (a) wife”, a nominal sentence, “is” understood. iḫuzma is aḫāzum “to take” (here “to take in marriage”) in the preterite, with -ma (iḫuz; the perfect would have the -ta- after the first sign); iškun is šakānum “to set, place”, so lā iškun is “he did not set down”. riksātiša is “her bonds”, the contracts that make a marriage binding; the same noun, riksātum, is “contracts” in the earlier laws. zinništum “woman” is written with the single sign SAL (Harper’s zinništum for the plate’s one sign), the same sign that spells aššatum “wife” in §26–41 and again at XXII 75 (aššatim): only the context says “woman” or “wife”. šī is “she, that”, the feminine of šū.

sentences.i: If a man’s wife is caught lying with another male, they shall bind them and throw them into the water.
sentences.n: Adultery, and the verdict is drowning, stated plainly. zikārum is “male”, šanûm “other, second”; ina itūlim is “in lying (together)”. Harper prints i-tu-lim here but u-tu-lim at XXI 72 (§131); both are as printed. ittaṣbat is the N-stem perfect of ṣabātum “to seize”, a passive: “was seized, caught” (the N-stem passive). ikassûšunūtima: the verb is probably kasûm “to bind” (Harper’s i-ka-zu spells it with the ZU sign, read su here; the verb is not certain), then -šunūti “them” and -ma, so “they shall bind them and”. inaddûšunūti is the same verb as inaddûšu in §127, nadûm “to throw”, now with “them”: “they shall throw them”. ana mê is “into the water”; mû, “water”, has the plural form mê. The two are thrown in together, the wife and her partner.

sentences.i: If a man has held down a man’s wife — one who has not known a male and is living in her father’s house —
sentences.n: A law about force, and the text states it without softening. ša zikaram lā īdûma is “who (has) not known a male”: edûm “to know”, subjunctive -u after ša, then -ma. ina bīt abiša wašbat “in her father’s house she dwells”: wašbat is the stative of wašābum, “she is living”; bīt, “house of”, is the construct of É. ukabbilšima is Harper’s u-kab-bil-ši-ma: the verb is kabālum in the D-stem, “to bind, hold fast”, with -ši “her” and -ma. “Held her down” is the sense taken here, not certain. The sign read kab is no. 46 of Harper’s List of Signs (kab), and the plate shows a sign of that shape in that place (XXI 60). The text calls her “a man’s wife” and says she is still living in her father’s house; it says no more about her situation. The law runs on into the next unit.

sentences.n: A long “if”, built from §134 with a new clause. ana pānīšu is literally “before him, to his face”; the sense taken here is “before his return”, UNCERTAIN as to the exact force (“before him” itself says nothing about a return). pānum is “face, front”. īterubma is erēbum “to enter” in the perfect with -ma (cf. the plain īterub in §133A). The unit ends on that -ma: the sentence goes on with the children and the husband’s return. Everything else is as in §134. Notice the pattern of the whole captivity block: a conditional with one condition per law, each ending in a verdict about the wife.

sentences.i: If a man has set his face to divorce a šugītum who has borne him children, or a wife who has provided him with children,
sentences.n: The divorce laws begin. šugītum is written with ŠAL (the woman-sign, a determinative here) before šu-gi₄-tim (Harper prints šu-ge-tim): Harper’s ge is his sign no. 122 (gi, GE), the sign the plate shows here (XXII 74), the same as the GE of MAL.GE.A in §110: a class of woman named only here, whom the law sets beside an ordinary wife as one who may bear children; her exact status is UNCERTAIN. ša mārī ūlidušum is “who (has) borne children to him” (walādum, subjunctive -u before -šum “to him”, so ūlidušum); ulu is “or” (the two kinds of woman); ušaršušu is the Š-stem of rašûm “to have, acquire”, ušarši + the subjunctive -u + -šu “him”, “who has made him acquire (children)”, the same sense in other words; the analysis of the ending is UNCERTAIN. The idiom is ezēbim pānīšu ištakan, “he has set his face to divorce”: ezēbum “to leave, divorce” (Harper’s e-ṣi-bi-im spells the ZI sign as ṣi, said zi), pānum “face”, and šakānum “to set”. Harper prints one a-na only, before the woman; ezēbim has none of its own.

sentences.i: If there is no bride-price, he shall give her one mina of silver as a divorce payment.
sentences.n: A short law, with the sums fixed. tirḫatum lā ibašši is “bride-price there is not”: lā ibašši, as in §134. The amount is I MA.NA KÙ.BABBAR-im, which Harper writes I ma-na kaspim: I is the sign for one (the plate has one wedge), ma-na “mina”, kaspim “of silver”, so ištēn mana kaspim, “one mina of silver”. ana uzubbîm is “as a divorce payment”: uzubbûm is the sum paid at a divorce (a rarer word, taken here from the context; UNCERTAIN as to the exact meaning). inaddiššim is as in §138. One mina is about half a kilogram of silver, 60 shekels.

sentences.i: If he is a commoner, he shall give her one-third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: The sum drops for a commoner. šumma muškēnum is “if (he is) a commoner”: muškēnum, written MAŠ.EN.KAK, the code’s second rank, with no verb, “is” understood, the sentence standing on its own like §128. The fraction is Harper’s ⅓ ma-na kaspim: ⅓ is the plate’s fraction-sign (the same sign as in §114 and §116, spoken šalšāt (?), reconstructed), mana “mina”, kaspim “of silver”; one third of a mina is twenty shekels. inaddiššim is as in §138–139. With this law the part ends.

glossary.târum-D: D-stem of târum: to give back: turru “taken away/captured”; utarrūšumma “they shall return (it) to him” · utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · turrim (infinitive, tu-ur-ri-im): ana turrim “for repaying, to give back”; utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · uttēr (ut-te-ir, perfect) “he has given back”: the same verb as utâr
glossary.ubānum: finger: ubānam ušatrīṣma “he made a finger point (at)” (the idiom for an accusation); ubānum, ubānam
glossary.ugbabtum: UNCERTAIN: a priestess, written ŠAL.NIN.AN (Harper aššatum NIN.AN; NIN.AN is later written NIN.DINGIR, “lady of the god”); Harper gives no reading and translates only “a priestess”, later editions read ugbabtum, and the ŠAL may be only the woman-sign. The reading rests on the sign group and the context, not on a spelled word · here (§127) NIN.AN alone, with no ŠAL before it: ugbabtim “of a priestess”, still read ugbabtum, UNCERTAIN as before (Harper gives no reading)
glossary.ulu: or (u-lu, a conjunction, “or … or”): ulu … ulu “either … or”, “or … or”, linking the clauses of a list
glossary.uzubbûm: UNCERTAIN: divorce payment, severance (uzubbûm): ana uzubbîm “as a divorce payment” (u-zu-ub-bi-im, genitive after ana); the reading is Harper’s and the word is rare
glossary.wabālum: to bring, carry: itbalam “he brought”, lū ublam “let me bring” · ublū (preterite, plural, in a ša-clause) “(the water) carried off”
glossary.walādum: to bear, give birth to: ūlidušum (ul-du-šum) “(whom) she bore to him” (preterite ūlid, the long ū of a w-initial verb, with the subjunctive -u and the dative -šum; Harper’s spelling is shortened, so the vowels of the form are UNCERTAIN)
glossary.wardum: male slave (ARAD) · warad (ARAD, no ending written) “male slave of …”, wardam (ARAD-am)
glossary.warki: after, behind: warkišu “after him, in his absence”
glossary.wašābum: to sit: ul uššab “he shall not sit” (the stone writes uš-ta-ab — a carver’s slip Harper flags) · to dwell: wāšbum (participle, contracted) “the dweller, the tenant” (a conjectured reading, aš-bu-u[m]); wa… “dwell-” in broken forms · stative wašbat (wa-aš-ba-at) “she dwells, lives”: ša ina gagîm lā wašbat “who does not live in the cloister” · stative wašib (wa-ši-ib-ma, with -ma) “he is staying”: ina ḫarrānim wašib “he is staying on the road”
glossary.wašārum: D-stem (w)uššurum “to release, set free”: ūtaššar “he shall be released” · the form ūtaššar (ū-ta-aš-šar) is the Dt, the t-form of the D-stem, in the present: “he shall be released”; the “D-stem” named above is the stem family, and this form is its t-form (Dt)
glossary.zakārum: to name, declare: izzakar “he named”, izakkarma “he shall declare, and”
glossary.zikārum: male, man as a sex (opposed to a woman): zikaram, zikārim “a male”
glossary.zinništum: woman (written with the single sign SAL, ŠAL in Harper): zinništam, zinništim, zinništum
glossary.zittum: share, portion (written ḪA.LA): zittašu, zittišu “his share” · zittam (ṣi-it-tam, the ZI sign read ṣi by Harper and zi here, as in ezēbim) “a share”: zittam kīma aplim ištēn “a share like one heir’s”
glossary.zêrum: to hate, loathe: izīrūma “he hated, and” (preterite izīr + the subjunctive -u after aššum + -ma, in “he hated his city and fled”); the reading rests on the context
glossary.ālum: city (URU): ālum u rabiānum “the city and the mayor”
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him · iššakkan (iš-ša-ak-ka-an, N-stem present) “it shall be put”: ul iššakkan “it shall not be put (in the account)”
glossary.šalālum-N: to be carried off (as booty; said of a man taken away): iššalilma “he was carried off, and” (N-stem preterite, with -ma); the G-stem šalālum is “to plunder, carry off”
glossary.šalāmum-D: D-stem of šalāmum “to be whole, sound”: to make good, restore (Harper: “to restore”): ušallamma (u-ša-lam-ma) “he shall make good, and”
glossary.šanûm: another, a second one: ana šanîm “to another”, šanûm “another man”
glossary.šarrum: king: šarrum “the king”, šar-ri-im “of the king”
glossary.šeriqtum: dowry, what the bride brings from her father’s house (§138 ša ištu bīt abiša ublam “which she brought from her father’s house”): šeriqtam “the dowry”, šeriqtaša “her dowry”. Harper reads it with q (še-ri-iq-ta-ša, the sign IG read iq) and later editions with k; UNCERTAIN in the form, the meaning rests on §138
glossary.šugītum: UNCERTAIN: a class of woman named in §137, written {šal}šu-gi₄-tim (Harper prints šu-ge-tim): šugītim “(to) a šugītum”; the law sets her beside an ordinary wife as a woman who may bear children; her exact status is not known
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šunūti: them (masculine plural, accusative): ṣarrūtim šunūti “those criminals”
glossary.šuāti: that, the aforesaid · as the independent pronoun “him”: šuāti u bīšašu “him and his goods”
glossary.šī: she, that (feminine pronoun, as the independent word): ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA šī “that tavern-keeper”; the masculine is šū
glossary.ḫāwirum: UNCERTAIN: husband (Harper ḫāwirum, from a root also read ḫāʾirum): ḫāwiriša “her husband”, at §135 the husband she had before (so Ungnad’s 1909 glossary: the first husband a girl marries); a rarer word than mutum
glossary.ṣabātum: to seize: iṣṣabat, ṣabtu · stative with the subjunctive -u: adi kirâm ṣabtu “as long as he holds the orchard” (with Harper’s kirûm: “as long as the orchard is held”) · iṣṣabtamma (iṣ-ṣa-ab-tam-ma) “she seized (them), and” (perfect with the ventive -am and -ma): lā iṣṣabtamma “and she did not seize” · iṣbassuma (iṣ-ba-zu-ma, ZU for -ssu) “it seized him, and” (preterite iṣbat + -šu + -ma), of a debt seizing a man · iṣṣabtūšu (iṣ-ṣa-ab-tu-šu) “they seized him” (perfect, plural, with -šu “him”); iṣṣabat (iṣ-ṣa-ba-at) “he has seized (his wife)” (perfect)
glossary.ṣabātum-N: to be seized, caught (N-stem, passive of ṣabātum): iṣṣabit “she was caught” (preterite, in lā iṣṣabit); ittaṣbat “she was caught” (perfect)
